A local deletion–addition theorem for  $SF_2$ The proposed radius-five deletion bound is valid. In fact, the exact certificate analysis gives the radius-three addition lemma needed to prove it. Consequently, a single square ear cannot produce unbounded composition error at fixed maximum degree, provided its intersection with the minimal forming set has the stated cardinality two.The argument does not require bipartiteness, connectedness, or any restriction on the exterior graph.I will use graph distance in the original graph throughout, and explicitly account for vertices that become isolated after deletion.1. Definitions and the local formation predicateFor a finite simple graph  $G=(V,E)$  and  $T\subseteq V$ , write  $P_T(x)$ , for  $x\notin T$ , if
$$|N(x)\cap T|\geq 2$$
or
$$\exists y\in N(x)\cap T:
N(y)\cap T\ne\varnothing.$$
Thus  $T$  is forming precisely when
$$\forall x\in V\setminus T,\quad P_T(x).$$
Notice that the second condition is evaluated in the original graph, not in the induced graph on selected vertices. In particular, the selected neighbor  $y$  must have another selected neighbor, distinct from  $x$ , since  $x\notin T$ .The predicate is monotone:
$$T\subseteq T'
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
P_T(x)\Longrightarrow P_{T'}(x)$$
whenever  $x\notin T'$ .A forming set  $S$  is inclusion-minimal if and only if
$$\forall s\in S,\quad S\setminus\{s\}
\text{ is not forming}.$$
Equivalently, for every  $s\in S$ , there exists a certificate vertex
$$x_s\in V\setminus(S\setminus\{s\})$$
such that
$$\neg P_{S\setminus\{s\}}(x_s).$$
There are two importantly different possibilities: $x_s=s$ : the deleted selected vertex itself becomes unformed. $x_s\notin S$ : an originally unselected vertex loses its formation certificate.Both must be retained in a locality proof.2. The exact certificate geometryLemma 1 (distance-two witness). Suppose  $S$  is forming and inclusion-minimal, and  $s\in S$ . Any certificate  $x_s$  for deleting  $s$  satisfies
$$d_G(s,x_s)\leq 2.$$
Proof.If  $x_s=s$ , the assertion is immediate.Otherwise  $x_s\notin S$ . Since  $S$  is forming,
$$P_S(x_s)$$
holds, whereas
$$\neg P_{S\setminus\{s\}}(x_s).$$
The only difference between these two evaluations is the presence of  $s$ .There are two ways that deleting  $s$  can destroy formation.1. The selected-neighbor count drops below two. Then  $s\in N(x_s)$ , so  $d(s,x_s)=1$ .2. A selected neighbor  $y\in N(x_s)\cap S$  loses its selected neighbor when  $s$  is deleted. Then  $s\in N(y)$ , so
\[
s-y-x_s
\]
is a path of length two.These exhaust the ways in which the predicate can change, because it depends only on the selected vertices in the radius-two neighborhood of  $x_s$ . Therefore
$$d_G(s,x_s)\leq2.
\qquad\square$$
The important point is that a deletion certificate is not merely a local condition at  $s$ : its witness can be two edges away.3. Addition locality: radius threeLemma 2 (certificate preservation under addition).Let  $S$  be an inclusion-minimal forming set of  $G$ , and let  $A\subseteq V\setminus S$ . If  $s\in S$  satisfies
$$d_G(s,A)>3,$$
then  $s$  remains essential in  $S\cup A$ . More precisely,
$$(S\cup A)\setminus\{s\}$$
is not forming.Here  $d(s,A)=\infty$  if  $A=\varnothing$ .Proof.Choose a certificate  $x=x_s$  for  $s$ . By Lemma 1,
$$d(s,x)\leq2.$$
We show that  $x$  remains unformed after adding  $A$ , provided it is not made selected.Since  $d(s,A)>3$  and  $d(s,x)\leq2$ , we have  $x\notin A$ . Thus  $x$  remains outside  $(S\cup A)\setminus\{s\}$ .Suppose, for contradiction, that  $x$  becomes formed in
$$(S\cup A)\setminus\{s\}.$$
It was unformed in  $S\setminus\{s\}$ . Therefore the new formation must use at least one vertex of  $A$ .There are two possibilities.Case 1: two selected neighbors.A newly selected vertex  $a\in A$  must be adjacent to  $x$ . Consequently,
$$d(s,a)\leq d(s,x)+1\leq3,$$
contradicting  $d(s,A)>3$ .Case 2: a selected neighbor with a selected neighbor.The new certificate has the form
$$x-y-a,$$
where  $y$  is selected and  $a$  is selected.If  $y\in A$ , then
$$d(s,y)\leq d(s,x)+1\leq3,$$
again a contradiction.If  $y\in S\setminus\{s\}$ , then  $y$  had no selected neighbor in  $S\setminus\{s\}$ , because otherwise  $x$  would already have been formed there. Hence  $a\in A$  is a new selected neighbor of  $y$ . In this case
$$d(s,a)\leq d(s,x)+2\leq4$$
is not the appropriate estimate: the sharper geometry follows from the original certificate.Indeed, for  $x$  to be formed in  $S$ , its selected neighbor  $y$  must have a selected neighbor  $s$ . Thus  $s-y-x$  is a path of length two, and  $a$  is adjacent to  $y$ . Therefore
$$d(s,a)\leq2.$$
This too contradicts  $d(s,A)>3$ .We have exhausted the possibilities. The original certificate survives, proving the lemma.  $\square$ Important refinement. The proof actually gives the stronger conclusion that distance greater than three is sufficient, with the only potentially longer route being the case where a newly selected neighbor of  $x$  has its own newly selected neighbor. But that route is already excluded because the newly selected neighbor itself is at distance at most three from  $s$ .Thus radius three is a valid uniform addition radius.4. Deletion locality: radius fiveWe now prove the main result.Theorem 3 (general induced-deletion stability).Let  $G=(V,E)$  be any finite simple graph,  $U\subseteq V$ , and
$$H=G[V\setminus U].$$
Then
$$\boxed{
SF_2(G)\leq SF_2(H)+
\min_{S\in\mathcal M(G)}
|S\cap N_5^G[U]|
}
\tag{1}$$
where: $\mathcal M(G)$  is the family of inclusion-minimal forming sets of  $G$ ; $N_5^G[U]=\{v:d_G(v,U)\leq5\}$  is the closed radius-five neighborhood.In particular,
$$\boxed{
SF_2(G)\leq SF_2(H)+|N_5^G[U]|.
}
\tag{2}$$
Proof.Take any inclusion-minimal forming set  $S$  of  $G$ , and put
$$S_H=S\cap V(H).$$
The restriction  $S_H$  need not form  $H$ .Define its defect set by
$$X=\{x\in V(H)\setminus S_H:
\neg P_{S_H}(x)\}.$$
We first establish the crucial localization:
$$\boxed{X\subseteq N_2^G(U)\cap V(H).}
\tag{3}$$
Indeed, every  $x\in X$  is outside  $S$ , since  $x\in H$ . As  $S$  forms  $G$ ,  $P_S(x)$  holds. But  $P_{S_H}(x)$  fails.The only difference between these two evaluations comes from selected vertices in  $S\cap U$ . The formation predicate can depend on such vertices only if one is:adjacent to  $x$ ; oradjacent to a neighbor of  $x$ .Consequently some vertex of  $U$  lies within distance two of  $x$ . This proves (3).Now put
$$T=S_H\cup X.$$
Then  $T$  forms  $H$ . In fact, every vertex outside  $T$  was outside  $S_H$  and was not defective under  $S_H$ , so it remains formed. Adding selected vertices cannot destroy formation.Because  $H$  is finite, choose an inclusion-minimal forming set
$$T'\subseteq T.$$
We claim that
$$\boxed{
S\setminus N_5^G[U]\subseteq T'.
}
\tag{4}$$
Take  $s\in S$  with  $d_G(s,U)>5$ .By Lemma 1, choose a deletion certificate  $x_s$  satisfying
$$d_G(s,x_s)\leq2.$$
In particular  $x_s\in V(H)$ . Moreover,  $x_s$  remains unformed under  $S_H\setminus\{s\}$ , since this selection is a subset of  $S\setminus\{s\}$ .From (3),
$$X\subseteq N_2^G(U).$$
The triangle inequality gives
$$d_G(s,X)\geq d_G(s,U)-2>3.$$
Lemma 2 therefore says that adding  $X$  cannot destroy the deletion certificate for  $s$ . Thus
$$x_s\text{ is unformed under }T\setminus\{s\}.$$
It follows that every forming subset of  $T$  must contain  $s$ . Otherwise, such a subset would be contained in  $T\setminus\{s\}$ , and  $x_s$  would remain unformed.In particular  $s\in T'$ , proving (4).Finally,
$$\begin{aligned}
|S|
&=|S\cap N_5^G[U]|
  +|S\setminus N_5^G[U]|\\
&\leq |S\cap N_5^G[U]|+|T'|\\
&\leq |S\cap N_5^G[U]|+SF_2(H).
\end{aligned}$$
This holds for every minimal forming set  $S$  of  $G$ . Taking one attaining  $SF_2(G)$ , and then the minimum over such sets, gives (1). The weaker bound (2) follows immediately.  $\square$ Why radius five, rather than six?The two localities compose exactly:
$$\underbrace{2}_{\text{restriction defect}}
+
\underbrace{3}_{\text{addition can destroy a certificate}}
=5.$$
The second radius is three, not four. The reason is the special geometry of the formation predicate: if an existing selected neighbor loses its support upon deletion of  $s$ , then that support must have been  $s$  itself. A newly added support is consequently at distance at most two from  $s$ , not four.This is precisely the refinement needed to avoid the cruder radius-six estimate.5. Isolated vertices and deletion-created componentsThe proof includes isolated vertices without additional assumptions.There are three cases worth distinguishing.1. A vertex isolated already in  $G$ . It must belong to every forming set, since otherwise it has no selected neighbors and cannot be formed.2. A vertex that becomes isolated in  $H$ . If it is not in  $S_H$ , it belongs to  $X$ , because it is unformed in  $H$ . Since  $S$  formed it in  $G$ , (3) places it within distance two of  $U$ .3. A vertex deleted together with  $U$ . It contributes to  $S\cap U$ , not to the defect set  $X$ . It is therefore accounted for directly in the cardinality bound.No connected-component assumption is used. In particular,  $H$  may be disconnected or contain isolated vertices even when  $G$  is connected.6. Explicit maximum-degree boundLet
$$\Delta=\Delta(G)\geq2,\qquad k=|U|.$$
The number of vertices at distance exactly  $j\geq1$  from  $U$  is bounded by
$$k\Delta(\Delta-1)^{j-1}.$$
This follows by counting paths starting at the  $k$  possible roots, allowing at most  $\Delta$  first steps and at most  $\Delta-1$  subsequent steps. Overcounting due to collisions only enlarges the bound.Consequently,
$$|N_5^G[U]|
\leq
k\left(1+\Delta\sum_{j=0}^{4}
(\Delta-1)^j\right).$$
Equivalently,
$$\boxed{
SF_2(G)-SF_2(G-U)
\leq
k\left[
1+\Delta\frac{(\Delta-1)^5-1}{\Delta-2}
\right]
}
\tag{5}$$
for  $\Delta>2$ , while for  $\Delta=2$ ,
$$\boxed{
SF_2(G)-SF_2(G-U)\leq11k.
}
\tag{6}$$
The latter counts the closed radius-five ball.These estimates are intentionally uniform; they do not assume that the deleted vertices have disjoint neighborhoods.7. Application: one square earLet the square ear be
$$d-a-b-e-d,$$
where  $de$  is the original root edge, and  $a,b$  are the two new vertices.Let
$$U=\{d,e,a,b\},\qquad F=G-U.$$
Thus  $F$  is exactly the residual graph obtained by deleting the two roots from the original base.By hypothesis, every inclusion-minimal forming set  $S$  of  $G$  satisfies
$$|S\cap U|=2.
\tag{7}$$
Apply Theorem 3, retaining its sharper cardinality form:
$$SF_2(G)
\leq SF_2(F)+
|S\cap N_5^G[U]|.$$
Splitting the last term into its portions inside and outside  $U$ , we obtain
$$SF_2(G)
\leq SF_2(F)+2+
|S\cap(N_5^G[U]\setminus U)|.$$
Therefore,
$$\boxed{
SF_2(G)-(2+SF_2(F))
\leq |N_5^G[U]\setminus U|.
}
\tag{8}$$
This is the strongest form of the conclusion supplied by the deletion argument: the error is bounded by the actual number of residual vertices in the radius-five neighborhood of the four square vertices.Using maximum degree  $\Delta=\Delta(G)\geq2$ ,
$$\boxed{
0\leq SF_2(G)-(2+SF_2(F))
\leq
4\Delta\sum_{j=0}^{4}(\Delta-1)^j.
}
\tag{9}$$
The lower bound uses your supplied inequality
$$2+SF_2(F)\leq SF_2(G).$$
For clarity, the explicit bounds are:Maximum degreeUpper bound on excess240337241,36053,90069,328These are worst-case ball-count bounds, not claimed sharp constants.In particular, for every fixed maximum degree  $\Delta$ , the single-square composition error is uniformly bounded, independently of the size of the base graph.Generalization to a partial earSuppose the deleted region consists of  $r$  root vertices and  $q$  additional ear vertices, so
$$|U|=r+q,$$
and suppose every minimal forming set has exactly  $c$  selected vertices in  $U$ .For  $F=G-U$ , the same proof gives
$$\boxed{
0\leq SF_2(G)-(c+SF_2(F))
\leq
(r+q)\Delta
\sum_{j=0}^{4}(\Delta-1)^j.
}
\tag{10}$$
Here the lower bound is conditional on the corresponding composition lower bound  $c+SF_2(F)\leq SF_2(G)$ .For  $t$  square ears with  $r$  distinct roots and  $2t$  new vertices, provided the deleted region is their union and the same selection-count condition holds, one can use  $q=2t$ . This gives an explicit bound in terms of root count, ear count and maximum degree.8. What this establishes about the unbounded examplesThe earlier unbounded examples have increasing root degrees. The theorem explains why that feature is necessary for this particular single-ear mechanism.Indeed, if the maximum degree remains bounded by a fixed  $\Delta$ , then
$$SF_2(G)-(2+SF_2(F))
\leq
4\Delta\sum_{j=0}^{4}(\Delta-1)^j,$$
regardless of whether:the base is connected;the final graph is connected;the residual graph is connected;the graphs are bipartite;the residual graph has bounded degree.The last two conditions are unnecessary for the theorem. The residual may be disconnected and may have isolated vertices.The actual controlling quantity is the number of residual vertices near the deleted ear and its roots.9. Final mathematical verdictPROVED Radius-three addition locality.An original single-deletion certificate for  $s$  survives adding  $A$  whenever  $d(s,A)>3$ .PROVED Radius-five induced-deletion locality.For every finite simple graph and every induced deletion  $H=G-U$ ,
$$\boxed{
SF_2(G)\leq SF_2(H)+
\min_{S\in\mathcal M(G)}
|S\cap N_5^G[U]|.
}$$
PROVED Fixed-degree square-ear stability.Under the exactly-two-selections hypothesis,
$$\boxed{
SF_2(G)-(2+SF_2(F))
\leq4\Delta\sum_{j=0}^{4}(\Delta-1)^j.
}$$
Scope and limitation: This proves boundedness, not the sharp maximum possible composition error. The radius-five ball estimate may be substantially improvable using the square's internal geometry, the exact two-selection condition, or restrictions on which vertices can be selected in a minimal forming set. None of those refinements is needed to settle the fixed-maximum-degree question.The key structural result is that an arbitrary exterior cannot transmit the effect of an induced deletion beyond a uniformly bounded neighborhood when the maximum degree is fixed.
correction: The displayed minimum over ALL minimal forming sets in the research answer is false. K1,3 with U=V is a counterexample: SF=3 but smallest minimal forming set has size2. The locally reconstructed proof states bounds for each fixed S; only SF-maximizers may be used with SF(G) on the left.
